consensus_summary: All three blind responses converge on the Holy Spirit (indwelling presence, anointing, empowerment) as the dominant meaning of lamp oil, chiefly via Matthew 25 read with Zechariah 4 and the tabernacle lamp texts. Recognized alternatives include genuine faith/grace, good works or charity (patristic strands), the Word of God (minority), joy/gladness, and a non-allegorical 'preparedness' reading; two of three responses judge there is no fully settled consensus, but the Spirit reading is clearly the recognizable common view.
book_summary: The book defines lamp oil as the commandment's truth and correction received and laid up inwardly until it governs the life — proven, tested obedience stored within — with the resulting light being that obedience made visible as an example to others. It explicitly flags the Holy Spirit (anointing, consecration, empowering) as merely the 'commonly taught' view it is departing from.
rationale: The book acknowledges the consensus reading (oil = Holy Spirit) and deliberately displaces it with a different referent: internalized commandment/truth/correction issuing in proven obedience. This is not a mere refinement of the Spirit reading; it substitutes the word-and-obedience complex for the Spirit as the oil's referent. While the book's claim has family resemblance to two minority alternatives noted by the blind responses (the Word of God as fuel; good works as oil), its central formulation — correction/reproof stored as tested obedience — is not what any response treats as the recognizable common view, and the book itself frames it against the common teaching. That is the definition of DIVERGENT rather than NOVEL, since the displaced view is clearly recognizable in the consensus.
strongest_objection: Zechariah 4:6 ('Not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit') and Ezekiel 36:27 ('I will put my spirit within you'), both printed with the entry, most naturally identify the lamp's supply with God's Spirit rather than with internalized commandments, so the book's own proof texts partly reinforce the consensus it rejects; moreover, no verse explicitly equates lamp oil with obedience — the identification rests on chaining Proverbs 6:23 (commandment = lamp), Psalm 141:5 (reproof = excellent oil), Proverbs 21:20 (oil stored by the wise), and Psalm 119:11 (word hid in the heart), an inferential composite rather than a direct statement.
